newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan urged by bourse to divest share portfolio.
newsitem.headline: Jordan urged by bourse to divest share portfolio.

text.p: Jordan's stock market director said on Monday the government should seize on an unprecedented buying spree by emerging funds to start a long-delayed divestment of its vast share portfolio.

Wahib Shair, director general of the Amman Financial Market, said the government should take advantage of a two-week buying spree which sent prices soaring to their highest levels in two years to start unloading shares.

"Now is the opportunity. The natural thing is that the government responds. The government... has already publicly committed itself to privatisation, and it would not be strange if it finds a way to sell part of its stocks," Shair said.

The government, which says it is serious about moving ahead on state selloffs as part of a privatisation drive, retains holdings estimated to be around 40 percent of the market's capitalisation of 3.2 billion dinars ($4.5 billion).

While the market has shot up, the state-owned Jordan Investment Corporation and government pension fund have sat on the sidelines in a market which many criticise as lacking major local institutional market movers.
All three main stocks which foreigners have focused on so far -- Jordan Cement, Arab Potash and Jordan Phosphate Mines -- have state holdings which exceed 50 percent.
Foreign funds have complained of lack of availability of stock because many of those most in demand have already reached their ceiling in a limited free float of traded stock.
They say sustaining the global fund buying depends on lifting a 50 percent foreign ownership ceiling and a drive to sell the state's vast stock portfolio to alleviate limited supplies.
Majority state-owned Arab Potash, one of Jordan's top export earners, has only 0.06 percent of its shares freely available for trade while Jordan Phosphates has around 5 percent.

Shair told Reuters that the extent of the latest foreign buying spree had made it more pressing for the government to act on proposals the bourse had submitted on how to expand foreign ownership beyond a 50 percent ceiling.

The bourse recommended three options: expand the current 50 percent foreign ownership ceiling to 70 percent, exclude sizeable Arab state holdings from the 50 percent reckoning, or to eliminate the ceiling for some shares, Shair said.
"The entry of the foreigners into the market has shown how serious and pressing the matter is," Shair said adding the government had promised to deliberate quickly.
Official data shows foreign purchases in the last two weeks alone was nearly double the whole of last year's international buying, totalling 9.6 million dinars ($13.5 million).

Tight supply of shares is behind the fast rise in prices, estimated to have gone up as much as eight percent within the brief span of two weeks, which analysts say is not sustainable if funds pull back.
The official 60-share index on Monday fell 0.82 percent to 163.00 points on Monday after foreign fund buying momentum weakened after two weeks of stepped up purchases.
"The price rise was a result of tight supplies of shares as well as anxiety by foreign investors to position themselves in select stock," said Omar al-Masri of Atlas Investment Group.

Echoing the view of many fund managers, Masri said the bulk of foreign demand has not been appeased yet but to raise market liquidity over the coming months the government had to start divesting its holdings to satisfy fund appetite.
